title: He must increase (John 3:22–30)
hookLine: John the Baptist rejoices to become less

cards: Someone starts something: a band, a small business, a ministry at church, a club at school. It grows because of them. Then a newcomer shows up, and people start following the newcomer instead.
Friends come by, upset on the founder's behalf: everyone's going over there now.
Today John the Baptist's disciples bring him exactly that news, about the man he pointed out at the Jordan, and his answer turns their worry inside out.

teach.b: Jesus and his disciples are baptizing in Judea, and John is still baptizing nearby. His disciples come to him: Rabbi, the one you pointed out across the Jordan is baptizing, and all men come to him. There's worry in it.
John answers first with a principle, in the Douay-Rheims: "A man cannot receive any thing, unless it be given him from heaven." Whatever we have is given. Then a picture from a wedding.
The bride belongs to the bridegroom.
His friend, the best man, doesn't sulk because the bride isn't his. He stands near, hears the bridegroom's voice, and is glad. This, John says, is my joy, and it is full.
Then the line: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Must. It isn't a resigned sigh.
In John's mouth it sounds like a plan, even a delight. Saint Augustine noticed something about the calendar.

The Church celebrates John's birth on June twenty-fourth, just after the longest day of the year, when daylight starts to shrink, and Jesus's birth in late December, just after the shortest day, when the light begins to grow.

teach.h: HE MUST INCREASE, BUT I MUST DECREASE.
teach.b: Augustine said the calendar itself preaches this verse: John's days decrease, Christ's increase. Where the dates came from is debated; Augustine simply read the fit as a sermon. Not every good thing needs your name on it.
Sometimes the way to love something is to step aside and be glad.

how: Catholics celebrate the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist on June 24 and Christmas on December 25, and preachers since Augustine have linked the two dates to John's words, he must increase, but I must decrease.

o: the pope who set Christmas in late December

games.q: the bridegroom's friend — tap the pairs.

s: John the Baptist resented Jesus's success
he says his joy is full, like the bridegroom's friend.
John says a man can receive nothing unless it's given from heaven
John 3:27: whatever we have is given.
Augustine linked the feast days to this verse
John's birth as days shorten, Christ's as days lengthen.

games.q: you're John the Baptist. your disciples tell you the crowds are leaving you for the one you pointed out. what do you say?
o: we need to win them back.
he must increase, but I must decrease.
I was here first; remember that.
games.why: John compares himself to the bridegroom's friend, glad to hear his voice: "He must increase, but I must decrease."

practice: Think of a recent win you were part of, a project, a family dinner, a team result, and find the person whose part got less notice than yours.
Picture what they did, and let yourself be glad about it the way the bridegroom's friend is glad, not grudging. If you pray, thank God for them.

wordCard.voice: Saint Augustine. The bishop who noticed that John's birthday falls after the longest day and Christ's after the shortest, the calendar itself preaching he must increase. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the Vulgate of John 3:30: he must increase. The line Augustine tied to the calendar.

carryVoice: Your line: glad to stand near. The friend's joy is full when the bridegroom is heard. Go gently.
